Between every two microtasks
Strictly before any microtask

questions.text: A queueMicrotask scheduled inside setTimeout runs after that timeout callback and before the next timer.
How do ECMAScript job queues relate to the browser event loop queues?
questions.answer: The JS spec defines Jobs and Job Queues (Promise Jobs). The host (browser, Node) decides when to run those jobs against its own work: timers, I/O, rendering. “Microtask vs macrotask” is the host model on top of JS jobs.

questions.text: What does an endless queueMicrotask(() => queueMicrotask(...)) chain do?
options: It starves macrotasks and rendering: the microtask queue never empties
After N steps it yields to setTimeout
It throws RangeError like stack recursion
It is automatically turned into a macrotask

questions.text: MutationObserver callbacks are queued as microtasks.
Why can a Promise created inside setTimeout beat the next setTimeout, but not the current timer callback?
questions.answer: The current timeout is the macrotask already running. A promise from it enqueues a microtask, which runs right after that callback and before the next macrotask. The next setTimeout waits for a new macro turn, so the then runs first.

questions.text: How does a then that returns Promise.resolve() differ from a then that returns a number, for the next then?
options: Returning a promise adds an extra unwrap microtask, so sibling microtasks already queued can slip in
There is no difference: both following thens are queued the same way
Returning a promise turns the rest of the chain into a macrotask
The number is ignored and the next then is not called

questions.text: A finite queueMicrotask chain, each step queueing the next, and a setTimeout(0) already queued:
options: The timer slips in after the first queueMicrotask
The timer runs only after the microtask chain finishes
The timer cancels the remaining microtasks
They run in parallel

questions.text: In the browser, where does a MessageChannel callback sit if postMessage, a microtask, and setTimeout(0) are all queued from the same synchronous turn?
options: Before microtasks
After every timer
After microtasks, but before the setTimeout(0) from that same turn
On the same microtask queue as then

questions.text: In the browser, a requestAnimationFrame scheduled from synchronous code next to setTimeout(0) runs…
options: Before any microtask
Strictly after that timer
Inside the current stack
After microtasks and before that timer

questions.text: Why isn’t then on an already fulfilled promise called on the same line?
options: A promise reaction is a job: it is queued, not called nested
then always waits for a setTimeout
You cannot subscribe to a fulfilled promise
It is called on the same line when the promise is fulfilled

options: nextTick always jumps ahead of any then
Promise reactions already queued finish first; that nextTick does not preempt them
They share one FIFO queue
nextTick inside then is a setImmediate

options: The caller receives a promise whose value is a Promise object
Returning a promise from an async function is forbidden
The outer promise waits for anotherPromise and settles with it
The outer promise fulfills immediately, without waiting

questions.text: A setTimeout(0) queued earlier from synchronous code, and a setTimeout(0) queued later from a microtask:
options: The timer from the microtask overtakes the one already queued
Both timers become microtasks
Timer order is random
The one queued first runs first

questions.text: What happens at await inner() inside an async function outer?
options: inner runs synchronously until its own await, and outer’s continuation is a microtask after inner’s promise
inner is not called until outer finishes
await inner() is the same as setTimeout(inner, 0)
inner’s code after await runs before outer’s synchronous start

options: Always escapes as a synchronous exception into the caller
Becomes a rejection of the returned promise and can surface as an unhandled rejection
Becomes a setTimeout
Is swallowed by the engine with no trace

options: Yes, on the same queue as then
Yes, and it runs before queueMicrotask
No: it is a host task and runs after microtasks are drained
It calls onmessage synchronously

options: Yes, setImmediate is always first
Yes, setTimeout is always first

No: from the top level their order is not guaranteed

The loop yields every iteration for then
The microtask queue runs in parallel
After 0 ms the loop yields to a timer

options: The second replaces the first
Both are microtasks, in subscription order
Run synchronously when then is called
The second becomes a macrotask

options: Promises first, then nextTick
They share one mixed queue
nextTick first, then promises, and only after that the next macrotask
nextTick waits for the next timer

options: rAF cuts into the middle of then
rAF runs synchronously inside the timer
rAF runs before then
then runs before rAF

options: catch receives the rejection as a microtask, and the next then receives whatever catch returned
The exception stops the process
The then after catch is never called
catch runs synchronously inside then

questions.text: What does it mean to drain the microtask queue?
options: Exactly one microtask is taken, then a macrotask is required
Microtasks run, including ones added along the way, until the queue is empty; the next macrotask waits
Microtasks run one at a time between lines of synchronous code
It applies only to setTimeout

questions.text: Returning Promise.resolve() from then and returning a number schedule the next then the same way relative to a sibling microtask already queued.
A finite chain of “a microtask queues a microtask” can delay a setTimeout(0) that is already queued.
In the browser, a MessageChannel onmessage handler is a microtask.
In the browser, a requestAnimationFrame scheduled from synchronous code next to setTimeout(0) runs before that timer.
then on an already fulfilled promise runs synchronously.
In Node.js, a nextTick scheduled inside a Promise.then runs before other then callbacks already queued.
return somePromise from an async function gives the caller a nested promise as the value, without waiting for it.
A setTimeout(0) from a microtask jumps ahead of a setTimeout(0) already in the timer queue.
Already queued microtasks cannot start while a synchronous loop still holds the stack.
Two then callbacks on one fulfilled promise run in subscription order.
In Node.js, after a setTimeout callback, nextTick callbacks queued there run before Promise.then callbacks queued there.
In the browser, a requestAnimationFrame scheduled inside setTimeout runs before a Promise.then from that same callback.
An exception inside then rejects that then’s promise and does not throw into the outer stack.
In Node.js, setImmediate and setTimeout(0) from the top level of a script always run in a fixed order.
await continues the function in the same call-stack turn as the code before await.
Promise jobs in the ECMAScript spec are setTimeout.
Evaluating await inner() does not call inner until outer finishes.
An unhandled rejection from an async function reaches the caller as a synchronous throw.
Why does returning a promise from then delay the next then more than returning a number?
questions.answer: A number is passed to the next reaction in one microtask. A returned promise still has to be unwrapped by another job, and microtasks already queued can run during that extra step.

questions.text: What does draining the microtask queue mean in practice?
questions.answer: Every current microtask is taken, including ones they add, until the queue is empty. The next macrotask and the render step wait for that.

questions.text: Why can a MessageChannel callback in the browser run before a timer that was queued before postMessage?
questions.answer: A port message is a host task, not a microtask. In this model it is taken after microtasks and before the timer queue, so it beats a setTimeout(0) from the same synchronous turn.

questions.text: Where does requestAnimationFrame sit relative to setTimeout(0) in this quiz’s browser model?
questions.answer: After microtasks are drained and before a timer queued in the same synchronous turn. Inside a timer that is already running, a then queued there still runs before an rAF queued there.

questions.text: Why doesn’t the spec call a promise reaction directly on the stack?
questions.answer: A reaction is a job. It is queued so then does not nest into the current stack and turn a long chain into synchronous recursion.

questions.text: Why is “nextTick in Node always runs before promises” too rough?
questions.answer: From synchronous code, and after a macrotask, the nextTick queue is drained before promises. A nextTick queued from inside a then does not preempt promise reactions that are already queued.

questions.text: Why doesn’t return otherPromise from an async function nest a promise inside a promise?
questions.answer: An async function adopts the returned promise: the outer promise waits for it and settles the same way. The caller’s then sees the final value, not a Promise object.

questions.text: Can a microtask reorder timers that are already queued?
questions.answer: No. A new setTimeout joins the back of the timer queue. The one queued earlier stays ahead, even if a microtask queued the later one.

questions.text: Why does a long synchronous loop freeze both timers and promises?
questions.answer: The event loop picks the next task only when the stack is empty. While a synchronous loop is running, no microtask, timer, or frame can start.

questions.text: Do two then callbacks on one promise replace each other?
questions.answer: No. Both stay. On a fulfilled promise they become two microtasks in subscription order.

questions.text: What is Node’s nextTick queue for, next to promise jobs?
questions.answer: It is an earlier host queue: after synchronous code and after a macrotask it is drained before promise microtasks. It is for a callback that must run before then, and it is still not a synchronous call.

questions.text: Why doesn’t the browser paint in the middle of then callbacks queued inside a timer?
questions.answer: The current macrotask finishes, then microtasks are drained, and only then can a render step happen. A then from the timer is part of that drain; the frame does not cut through it.

questions.text: How does catch keep a chain alive after a throw in then?
questions.answer: The throw rejects that then’s promise. catch receives the rejection as a microtask. If catch returns a value, the next then continues as a fulfillment, also as a microtask.

questions.text: Why shouldn’t you memorize an order of setImmediate and setTimeout(0) from Node’s main script?
questions.answer: From the top level, the timers phase and the check phase do not give one guaranteed order. Inside an I/O callback the order is different and stable, but that is another point in the loop.

questions.text: What happens to the stack at an await?
questions.answer: The function pauses and the stack unwinds to the caller. The continuation after await is a new microtask, not the tail of the same call.

questions.text: What does the JavaScript spec deliberately leave to the host?
questions.answer: Timers, I/O, painting, and when to run promise jobs. The spec describes jobs; the browser and Node weave them into their own loops.

questions.text: How do two async functions nest at await inner()?
questions.answer: The inner() call starts immediately and runs synchronously until its own await. outer waits for inner’s promise, and the code in outer after await becomes a microtask when inner settles.

questions.text: Why doesn’t a try/catch around an async call see a throw inside that function?
questions.answer: The call returns a promise and does not throw synchronously. The throw rejects that promise. You catch it with a catch on the promise, not with the outer try/catch.
